newsitem.title: CHINA: China promises no PLA troops on HK streets-Cook.
newsitem.headline: China promises no PLA troops on HK streets-Cook.

text.p: China has promised not to send People's Liberation Army troops onto the streets of Hong Kong in armoured cars, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Tuesday.
Cook said he had won the pledge from Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen who told him the force was strictly for external defence and not for internal security.
China sent 4,000 troops by land, sea and air into Hong Kong at dawn on Tuesday, just hours after Britain handed back the colony it had ruled for a century and a half.

The appearance of troops in Hong Kong is a highly charged political issue as memories of the 1989 Tiananmen massacre are still fresh in the minds of people who take to the streets in their thousands every year to commemorate the killings.
Cook said he welcomed the fact that a senior Chinese minister "has explicitly confirmed that the defence role of the PLA is solely external, not internal.
"Chinese troops should not be seen in marches or in armoured personnel carriers on the streets of Hong Kong," he told reporters.
Cook said he had also won assurances that elections would be held in Hong Kong by next May.
"Britain cannot turn its back on Hong Kong and will not," Cook said.
He said that if China did not fulfil its pledge to hold elections within a year "then certainly the United Nations is one useful forum in which we can explore that breach of the declaration".
The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration gave Hong Kong 50 years of autonomy under Beijing's "one country, two systems" formula.
"The message I leave with the people of Hong Kong is that we will walk with you through the 50 years for which terms of the handover remain in legal force," he said.
He told a news conference after the transfer-of-power ceremonies that he will return to Hong Kong at the end of the year and also visit Beijing "to make sure that our relations with both are strong".

Cook said he was flying back to Britain feeling that there were more pluses than minuses in the handover. He said he felt more encouraged about the future, particularly after he and Prime Minister Tony Blair met Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
But he did single out one big minus -- the dismissal of the elected legislative council -- and he praised leading Democrat Martin Lee for what he called a mature and restrained protest.
"Britain will continue to recognise him as the leader of the largest single party in Hong Kong and to meet with him to hear their views," he said.
"We will monitor them closely to satisfy ourselves that those elections are really free and fair," he said.

The watering down of Hong Kong's civil rights and democracy was fiercely opposed by Britain and by Hong Kong's own democracy movement which won 70 percent of the directly elected seats in the legislature in a vote held two years ago.
China has replaced the body with a provisional legislature handpicked by Beijing.
